Mesillat Yesharim 1:1:
An Explanation of the General Obligation of Man in His World
The foundation of piety and the root of perfect service [of God] is for a person to clarify and to ascertain what his obligation is in his world, and to what he needs to direct his attention and his aim in all that he labors all the days of his life.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:2: Now, what our Sages, of blessed memory, have taught us is that man was created for nothing other than to delight in the Lord and to derive pleasure from the splendor of His Presence (Shechinah), for this is the true delight and the greatest of all pleasures that can possibly exist. And the true place for this pleasure is the World to Come, for it is created with the preparation necessary for this purpose.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:3: But the path by which to reach this, our desired destination, is this world. This is what they said (Avot 4): This world is like a corridor before the World to Come.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:4: And the means that bring a person to this goal are the commandments which God, blessed be His Name, has commanded us. And the place for performing the commandments is only this world. Therefore man was placed in this world at first, so that by means of these opportunities afforded him here, he might reach the place that has been prepared for him, which is the World to Come, there to be sated with the good that he has acquired for himself through these means. This is what they said, of blessed memory (Eruvin 22a): Today to perform them, and tomorrow to receive their reward.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:5: And when you consider the matter, you will see that true perfection is only cleaving to Him, blessed be He, as King David used to say (Psalms 73:28): "But as for me, the nearness of God is my good." And he said (ibid. 27:4): "One thing have I asked of the Lord, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life..." for this alone is the true good. And anything else that people consider good is nothing but vanity and empty delusion.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:6: However, in order for a person to merit this good, it is fitting that he first labor and strive with all his effort to acquire it — that is, that he strive to cleave to Him, blessed be He, by means of deeds whose product is this very cleaving, and these are the commandments.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:7: Now, the Holy One, blessed be He, has placed man in a place with many things that distance him from Him, blessed be He, and these are the material desires, which, if he is drawn after them, cause him to become ever more distant from the true good.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:8: It follows, then, that he is truly placed in the midst of a mighty war, for all the affairs of the world, whether for good or for bad, are trials for a person: poverty on the one side and wealth on the other, as Solomon said (Proverbs 30:9): "lest I be full and deny, and say, Who is the Lord? Or lest I be poor and steal..."; tranquility on the one side and suffering on the other — so that the battle presses in upon him from front and back.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:9: And if he is a man of valor and wins the battle on every side, he will be the complete person who will merit to cleave to his Creator, and he will go out from this corridor and enter into the banquet hall, to bask in the light of life.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:10: And in the measure that he has subdued his inclination and his desires, and has distanced himself from the things that distance him from the good, and has striven to cleave to Him — accordingly will he attain Him and rejoice in Him.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:11: And if you delve further into this matter, you will see that the world was created for man's use. However, it stands in a great balance: for if a person is drawn after the world and grows distant from his Creator, then he becomes corrupted, and he corrupts the world along with himself; but if he governs himself and cleaves to his Creator, and uses the world only as an aid and support for the service of his Creator, then he is elevated, and the world itself is elevated together with him. For it is indeed a great elevation for all creatures to be in the service of the perfect man, sanctified with His holiness, blessed be He.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:12: This is like the matter which our Sages, of blessed memory, said concerning the light which the Holy One, blessed be He, hid away for the righteous, in these words (Chagigah 12a): "When it saw the light that the Holy One, blessed be He, had hidden away for the righteous, it rejoiced, as it is said (Proverbs 13:9), 'The light of the righteous rejoices.'"
Mesillat Yesharim 1:13: And concerning the stones of the place that Jacob took and set under his head, they said (Chullin 91b): Rabbi Yitzchak said, this teaches that they all gathered together into one place, each one saying, "Let the righteous one rest his head upon me."
Mesillat Yesharim 1:14: Now, our Sages, of blessed memory, alerted us to this very principle in the Midrash on Kohelet (Rabbah 7), where they said, in these words: "Consider the work of God, etc." (Ecclesiastes 7:13) — when the Holy One, blessed be He, created Adam, He took him and led him around all the trees of the Garden of Eden and said to him: See My works, how fine and praiseworthy they are; and all that I have created, I created for your sake. Take care that you do not corrupt and destroy My world.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:15: In sum: man was not created for the sake of his station in this world, but for the sake of his station in the World to Come; only that his station in this world is a means to his station in the World to Come, which is his ultimate purpose.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:16: Therefore you will find many statements of our Sages, of blessed memory, all in one and the same vein, comparing this world to a place and time of preparation, and the World to Come to a place of rest, where one eats what has already been prepared; and this is the meaning of what they said, that this world is like a corridor, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said: Today to perform them, and tomorrow to receive their reward (Avodah Zarah 3a). Whoever has toiled on the eve of the Sabbath will eat on the Sabbath. This world is like dry land, and the World to Come is like the sea, etc. (Kohelet Rabbah 1). And there are many statements of this kind.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:17: And you will truly see that no intelligent person could possibly believe that the purpose of man's creation is for his condition in this world; for what is human life in this world, or who is truly happy and at peace in this world? "The days of our years are seventy years, or if by reason of strength, eighty years; yet their pride is but labor and vanity" (Psalms 90:10),
Mesillat Yesharim 1:18: filled with so many kinds of pain, illnesses, sorrows, and troubles, and after all this, death. Not one in a thousand can be found for whom the world has multiplied pleasures and true tranquility. And even he — even if he reaches a hundred years — has already passed and vanished from the world.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:19: Moreover, if the purpose of man's creation had been for the sake of this world, there would have been no need for a soul so precious and so exalted — greater even than the angels themselves — to have been breathed into him.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:20: All the more so, since it finds no true satisfaction in any of the pleasures of this world. This is what they taught us in the Midrash on Kohelet, in these words (Kohelet Rabbah 6): "And also the soul is not satisfied" (Ecclesiastes 6:7) — to what may this be compared? To a commoner who married a princess: if he brings her everything in the world, it means nothing to her, for she is a princess. So too the soul — even if you were to bring it all the delicacies of the world, they would mean nothing to it. Why? Because it is of the celestial beings.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:21: And so our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:29): "Against your will you are formed, and against your will you are born" — for the soul does not love this world at all; rather, it despises it. If so, the Creator, blessed be He, would surely not have created a creature for a purpose that runs contrary to its very nature and is repugnant to it.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:22: Rather, man's creation is for the sake of his station in the World to Come. And this is why this soul was given to him — for it is fitting for this soul to serve, and through it man will be able to receive his reward in its proper place and time, so that it will not be a thing repugnant to his soul, as this world is, but on the contrary, beloved and cherished by it. And this is simple to understand.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:23: Now, once we know this, we will immediately understand the gravity of the commandments that are upon us, and the preciousness of the service that is in our hands; for these are the means that bring us to true perfection, without which it cannot be attained at all.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:24: However, it is known that the goal is reached only through the combined force of all the means that exist and that serve to attain it; and according to the strength of the means and their use, so will be the goal that results from them. And any small variance found among the means — its consequence will be verified with certain clarity when the time comes for the goal, which results from the combination of them all, as I have written; and this is clear.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:25: From this it is certain that the precision required in the matter of the commandments and the service must be of the utmost exactness, just as those who weigh gold and pearls are exact because of their great preciousness; for their outcome results in true perfection and eternal preciousness, than which there is no greater preciousness.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:26: We thus learn that the primary purpose of man's existence in this world is solely to fulfill the commandments, to serve God, and to withstand trial;
Mesillat Yesharim 1:27: and the pleasures of the world should be to him only a help and support, so that he may have contentment and peace of mind, in order that he may be able to devote his heart to this service that is incumbent upon him;
Mesillat Yesharim 1:28: and it is truly fitting that all his intention should be directed solely toward the Creator, blessed be He, and that he should have no other purpose in anything he does, whether small or great, except to draw near to Him, blessed be He, and to break down all the barriers that separate him from his Maker — namely, all matters of materiality and whatever depends on them — until he is drawn after Him, blessed be He, literally like iron after a magnet.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:29: And whatever he can think of as a means toward this closeness, he should pursue it and hold fast to it and not let it go.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:30: And whatever he can think of as an obstacle to this, he should flee from it as one flees from fire, as it is said (Psalms 63:9): "My soul cleaves after You; Your right hand upholds me,"
Mesillat Yesharim 1:31: since his coming into the world is for no other purpose than this, namely, to attain this closeness by rescuing his soul from all that hinders and corrupts it.
Mesillat Yesharim 1:32: And now that we have known and clarified for ourselves the truth of this general principle, we should investigate its particulars according to their levels, from the beginning of the matter to its end, as Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair arranged them in his statement which we already cited in our introduction, and they are: Watchfulness (zehirut), Alacrity (zerizut), Cleanliness (nekiyut), Abstinence (perishut), Purity (taharah), Piety (chassidut), Humility (anavah), Fear of Sin (yirat chet), and Holiness (kedushah).
Mesillat Yesharim 1:33: And now let us explain them one by one, with the help of Heaven.
Mesillat Yesharim 2:1:
An Explanation of the Trait of Watchfulness (Zehirut)
The matter of watchfulness is that a person should be watchful in his deeds and his affairs — that is, that he should reflect upon and examine his deeds and his ways, whether they are good or not, so as not to abandon his soul to the danger of ruin, God forbid, and so that he does not proceed along the path of his habit like a blind man in the darkness.
Mesillat Yesharim 2:2: Now, this is a matter which reason certainly obligates. For since a person has understanding and intelligence to save himself and to flee from the ruin of his soul, how could it be that he would want to shut his eyes to his own salvation,
Mesillat Yesharim 2:3: there is surely no worse lowliness and folly than this. And whoever does so is lower than the beasts and animals, which by their nature guard themselves, and so flee and run away from anything that appears to them to be harmful to them.
Mesillat Yesharim 2:4: And one who goes about in his world without reflecting on whether his path is good or bad is like a blind man walking along the bank of a river, whose danger is certainly immense, and whose ruin is nearer than his salvation. For the lack of caution — whether due to natural blindness or due to willful blindness, that is, the closing of one's eyes by choice and desire — amounts to the same thing.
Mesillat Yesharim 2:5: Now, Jeremiah used to lament the wickedness of the people of his generation, because they were afflicted with the plague of this very trait — that they would shut their eyes to their own deeds, without paying attention to see what they were: whether they should be done, or whether they should be abandoned.
Mesillat Yesharim 2:6: And he said of them (Jeremiah 8:6): "No man repented of his wickedness, saying... everyone turned to his own course, like a horse rushing headlong into battle."
Mesillat Yesharim 2:7: That is, they pursued and went along in the headlong rush of their habit and their ways, without allowing themselves time to scrutinize their deeds and their ways; and so it turned out that they fell into wickedness without seeing it.
